content: Enterovirus 68 (EV-D68) is a member of the enterovirus genus within the Picornaviridae family. It is a non-enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus. Transmission occurs through aerosolized particles or direct contact between individuals. Although historically rare, its prevalence has been increasing in recent years. While it was initially considered a pediatric infection, recent data suggest a higher incidence in adults. Unlike other enteroviruses, EV-D68 predominantly causes respiratory disease. Common symptoms include cough, shortness of breath (dyspnea), and wheezing. Differential diagnosis should include other respiratory pathogens such as respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, parainfluenza virus, seasonal influenza B, coronavirus, and rhinovirus. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) using oral or nasopharyngeal swab specimens. Most cases are managed with supportive care on an outpatient basis. However, severe cases, particularly in individuals at extremes of age or with pre-existing pulmonary or systemic diseases, may require hospitalization, oxygen supplementation, or mechanical ventilation. EV-D68 was first isolated in 1962 from hospitalized children in California presenting with pneumonia and bronchiolitis. It has recently gained clinical prominence, with a notable outbreak in the United States in September 2014 affecting 10 states. The virus exhibits a unique pathophysiology compared to other enteroviruses, with a strong tropism for respiratory mucosal cells and leukocytes. It replicates within leukocytes, facilitating viral dissemination and activation of endothelial cells, which attract additional leukocytes to the infection site. Transmission is believed to occur via respiratory secretions through aerosol or direct contact. EV-D68 belongs to the enterovirus genus, serotype D, and has a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome. It is acid-labile and grows optimally at lower temperatures. Its genome encodes a single polyprotein that is processed into various viral proteins. Viral serotyping is based on the VP1 gene, which encodes one of the four capsid proteins. Recent genomic rearrangements and deletions, particularly in untranslated regions (UTRs), have led to the classification of the virus into clades. The virus recognizes decay-accelerating factor (DAF) and sialic acid-containing receptors on cell surfaces, contributing to its tropism for lower respiratory tract mucosal cells and leukocytes. Differentiating EV-D68 from other diseases is critical, as it shares symptoms such as fever, cough, malaise, and rhinorrhea with infections caused by respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, parainfluenza virus, seasonal influenza B, coronavirus, and rhinovirus. Epidemiologically, EV-D68 is considered rare, with an unknown true incidence and prevalence. However, a recent rise in reported cases has been observed. While older data suggested a predominance in children aged 4 to 5 years, newer cases indicate a higher prevalence in adults. The infection is more common in males, with no significant variation by race or ethnicity. Risk factors for EV-D68 infection include poor hygiene practices, such as not covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing and inadequate handwashing. Extremes of age, pulmonary comorbidities (e.g., asthma, cystic fibrosis), and systemic comorbidities increase the risk of severe disease. The natural history of EV-D68 is not well understood due to limited data. Clinical presentations range from asymptomatic to severe respiratory symptoms requiring hospitalization. Prognosis is generally favorable, but fatalities have been reported. Approximately 16-21% of patients experience complications, such as secondary infections or severe pneumonia necessitating mechanical ventilation, particularly in vulnerable populations. Patients with EV-D68 infection typically present with symptoms of acute upper or lower respiratory tract infection, including cough, dyspnea, and fever. Physical examination findings often include fever, rapid breathing (tachypnea), skin rash, erythematous tonsils without exudates, and wheezing. Laboratory findings may reveal leukocytosis with lymphocyte predominance. RT-PCR assays of oral or nasopharyngeal swabs are usually positive, while viral culture is less commonly performed but can confirm the infectious agent. Serology tests have low sensitivity for diagnosing EV-D68. Chest X-rays may show abnormalities such as infiltrates, consolidation, atelectasis, or air trapping in patients with lower respiratory tract involvement. There is no specific antiviral treatment for EV-D68 infections. Most patients can be managed on an outpatient basis with supportive care. Severe cases may require hospitalization or admission to an intensive care unit for supportive management, including mechanical ventilation if necessary. Currently, no vaccines are available for EV-D68. Preventive measures include proper hand hygiene, avoiding contact with sick individuals, and disinfecting frequently touched surfaces. Future therapies for EV-D68 are under investigation. While management of enteroviruses is generally supportive, pharmacologic therapies are being explored. Immune globulin therapy has shown clinical and laboratory benefits in enterovirus infections. Antiviral medications, such as pleconaril, are being studied for severe infections caused by other enterovirus subtypes.
